title: Sona's bleeding feet
hookLine: the soft-footed monk who walked until his feet bled, and learned about the lute (Theragatha, Sona Kolivisa)

cards: Blood on a walking path. In the Vinaya's telling, a young man named Sona Kolivisa was raised so softly that hair grew on the soles of his feet.
Then he became a monk, and he walked up and down in meditation, back and forth, until his feet split open. The text says the path looked like a place where cattle are slaughtered.
He was giving it everything, and it wasn't working.

teach.h: I COULD GO HOME AND DO GOOD.
teach.b: First, the thought. Alone in the grove, Sona reasons with himself: I'm one of the disciples who strive hardest, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth.
I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. It's an honest thought, and the text doesn't mock it. Second, the question.
The Buddha knows his mind and comes to him, and he doesn't start with a teaching. He asks about Sona's old life.

teach.h: WERE YOU SKILLED AT THE LUTE?
teach.b: When you lived at home, were you skilled at the lute? Yes. When the strings were wound too tight, could it be played?
And tuned to an even pitch, neither too tight nor too slack? Then, yes. Third, the turn.

Just so, the Buddha says: effort pushed too hard runs into restlessness, and effort too slack runs into laziness. So set your effort evenly, tune your faculties to each other, and take your aim from there.
The answer came out of Sona's own hands.
Fourth, the sandals. In the Vinaya, after Sona's mind is freed, the Buddha offers him sandals for those soft feet.
Sona hesitates: people will say he gave up great wealth and now clings to footwear. He'll wear them only if every monk may. And the Buddha allows sandals for the whole order.
One man's bleeding feet became a kindness for everyone after him. The Theragatha keeps a song under his name, and behind it stands that lute.

how: The lute simile is retold in meditation teaching when a student is straining too hard or drifting too loose, and the Vinaya traces the monks' allowance of sandals to him.

o: a drum used to keep time in chanting

games.q: Sona and the lute: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha tells Sona to try harder
he tells him to tune his effort evenly, like a lute that's neither too tight nor too slack.
the Buddha starts by asking about Sona's old life
he asks whether Sona was skilled at the lute when he lived at home.
Sona keeps sandals for himself alone
in the Vinaya he'll wear them only if every monk may, and the Buddha allows them for the whole order.

games.q: you're Sona. your feet are bleeding, you've given everything, and your mind still isn't free. your family is rich. what do you do?
o: walk harder until something breaks open.
go home, enjoy the wealth and do good with it.
stay, and let the teacher retune you.
games.why: Sona considers going home. the Buddha comes, asks about the lute, and Sona sets his effort evenly. the text says his mind was then freed.

practice: Take your shoes off if you can, let your feet rest flat on the floor, and let the breath come at its own pace, not pulled long, not held short.

If you catch yourself trying hard to relax, that's a tight string, so let it slacken; if you drift off, that's a slack one, so come back to the soles of your feet. Somewhere between the two, there's an even note.

wordCard.voice: Vina. A lute: the instrument the Buddha used to teach Sona, who had walked until he bled, that effort is tuned, neither too tight nor too slack. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vina: the lute the Buddha asks Sona about, tuned neither too tight nor too slack.

carryVoice: Your line: not too tight. Effort, like a lute, gets tuned. That's day eight hundred eight.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 5.1 (Sona Kolivisa, the lute, the sandals)
